item.title: Zhuling AI Agent Framework: Java-Based Agent Scaffolding for Spring Boot Developers
item.description: Zhuling (铸灵) is a Java-based AI agent development framework built on SpringBoot 4.1 and Spring AI 2.0, offering zero-code agent configuration via YAML and DDD hexagonal architecture.
item.content:encoded:
Zhuling (铸灵) is a brand-new Java-based AI agent development framework created on July 28, 2026, that provides enterprise-grade scaffolding for building intelligent agents on the Spring Boot ecosystem. Built on SpringBoot 4.1.0 and Spring AI 2.0.1-SNAPSHOT, Zhuling distinguishes itself through a Domain-Driven Design (DDD) hexagonal architecture, zero-code agent configuration via YAML, and full support for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) across Local, SSE, and Stdio modes — making it one of the most architecturally ambitious Java AI agent frameworks to emerge in 2026.

What Is Zhuling and Why Does It Matter for Java AI Agent Development?

Zhuling (铸灵, meaning “forge the spirit”) is an open-source AI agent scaffolding framework for Java developers, licensed under Apache 2.0 and created by the developer known as Vinist. The framework is designed to dramatically reduce the boilerplate required to build, configure, and deploy AI agents within the Spring ecosystem. Its core value proposition is simple: define an agent in YAML, and Zhuling handles the rest — from LLM integration and tool registration to multi-agent orchestration and observable chat UI.

The framework matters because it targets a specific pain point in the Java AI landscape. While Python-based frameworks like LangChain and CrewAI have matured rapidly, Java developers have had fewer options that feel native to their ecosystem. Zhuling aims to change that by offering a Spring Boot-native experience with DDD-grade architecture from day one.

What Technical Stack Does Zhuling Use?

Zhuling is built on the absolute cutting edge of the Spring ecosystem:

Component Version Role
SpringBoot 4.1.0 Application framework and dependency injection
Spring AI 2.0.1-SNAPSHOT AI model integration and tool calling
JDK 21+ Virtual threads and modern Java features
Maven 3.8+ Build and dependency management
Architecture DDD Hexagonal Domain-driven design with strict dependency rules

The choice of SpringBoot 4.1.0 and Spring AI 2.0.1-SNAPSHOT places Zhuling at the bleeding edge — these are pre-release or very recent versions that give access to the latest AI capabilities but also mean the framework depends on evolving APIs. JDK 21 is required for virtual thread support, which enables efficient concurrent agent execution without the complexity of traditional thread management.

How Does Zhuling’s Zero-Code Agent Configuration Work?

Zhuling’s standout feature is its “zero-code Agent startup” approach. Instead of writing Java classes to define agent behavior, developers configure agents entirely through YAML files. Here is a conceptual example of what a Zhuling agent configuration looks like:

agent:
  name: "customer-support-agent"
  model:
    provider: "openai"
    model: "gpt-4o"
    temperature: 0.3
  tools:
    - mcp-local:
        class: "com.zhuling.tool.OrderLookupTool"
    - mcp-sse:
        url: "http://internal-api:8080/mcp/orders"
  skills:
    - name: "order-refund"
      script: "refund-flow.py"
  memory:
    type: "conversation-window"
    windowSize: 20

This YAML-driven approach means developers can define, test, and iterate on agent behavior without recompiling code. The framework reads the configuration at startup, wires together the LLM provider, tool registry, skill scripts, and memory strategy, then exposes the agent through a built-in observable chat UI.

What Is DDD Hexagonal Architecture and How Does Zhuling Implement It?

Zhuling adopts Domain-Driven Design (DDD) with a Hexagonal (ports and adapters) architecture. The dependency flow follows a strict unidirectional rule:

Trigger → API → Case → Domain ← Infrastructure

This means:

  • Trigger layer: Entry points (HTTP controllers, message listeners, scheduled tasks)
  • API layer: Application programming interfaces and DTOs
  • Case layer: Application use cases and orchestration logic
  • Domain layer: Core business logic and domain models (no external dependencies)
  • Infrastructure layer: External integrations (databases, LLM providers, MCP servers) — depends on Domain interfaces

The Domain layer is the heart of the system and has zero knowledge of external frameworks or infrastructure. This makes the domain logic testable in isolation and allows infrastructure implementations to be swapped without affecting business rules. For an AI agent framework, this means the agent’s core reasoning and tool-calling logic is cleanly separated from LLM provider implementations, MCP transport mechanisms, and persistence strategies.

How Does Zhuling Compare to Other Java AI Agent Frameworks?

The Java AI agent framework landscape has grown significantly in 2025-2026. Here is how Zhuling stacks up against the main competitors:

Feature Zhuling Spring AI Alibaba JetBrains Koog Embabel Agent Agents-Flex LangChain4j
GitHub Stars New (0) 10,463+ 4,480+ 3,824+ 1,048+ 12,000+
Created July 2026 2024 May 2025 April 2025 Jan 2024 2023
Zero-Code Config ✅ YAML-based ❌ Java code ❌ Kotlin code ❌ Kotlin code ❌ Java code ❌ Java code
DDD Architecture ✅ Hexagonal ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
MCP Support ✅ Local/SSE/Stdio ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌
Spring Native ✅ SpringBoot 4.1 ✅ Spring AI ❌ ✅ Spring ❌ ❌
Multi-Agent ✅ (Phase 7+) ✅ Graph-based ✅ ✅ ✅ Sub-agents ❌
JDK Requirement 21+ 17+ 17+ 17+ 8+ 8+
License Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0

Spring AI Alibaba (10,463+ Stars)

Alibaba’s official Spring AI extension is the most popular Java AI agent framework by a wide margin. It offers ReAct agents, multi-agent graph orchestration, and deep integration with Alibaba Cloud’s Tongyi Qianwen model. However, it requires Java code for agent definition and is tightly coupled to the Alibaba Cloud ecosystem.

JetBrains Koog (4,480+ Stars)

Koog is JetBrains’ JVM AI agent framework, written in Kotlin but Java-compatible. It is enterprise-ready, fault-tolerant, and supports MCP, multi-agent systems, and multiple LLM providers (Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic). Koog benefits from JetBrains’ AI product expertise but requires Kotlin or Java coding for agent setup.

Embabel Agent (3,824+ Stars)

Embabel is a fast-growing JVM agent framework with multi-agent orchestration and Spring integration. Created in April 2025, it has seen rapid adoption but similarly requires code-based agent definitions.

Agents-Flex (1,048+ Stars)

Agents-Flex positions itself as a lightweight alternative to Spring AI. It supports RAG, MCP, Skills, Text2SQL, and sub-agents. Created in January 2024, it is more mature than Zhuling but lacks the DDD architecture and zero-code configuration.

LangChain4j (12,000+ Stars)

The Java port of LangChain has the largest community and most extensive documentation. It supports RAG, tool calling, memory, and multiple LLM providers. However, it is not specifically an “agent framework” — it provides building blocks that developers assemble into agents through code.

What Are Zhuling’s Key Advantages?

Spring Ecosystem Integration: Zhuling is built natively on SpringBoot 4.1 and Spring AI 2.0, meaning it inherits Spring’s mature dependency injection, configuration management, and lifecycle features. Java developers familiar with Spring can start building AI agents without learning a new paradigm.

Configuration Simplicity: The YAML-driven agent definition is Zhuling’s strongest differentiator. In a landscape where every competing framework requires writing code to define agents, Zhuling’s approach allows non-specialist developers and DevOps teams to configure and deploy AI agents through configuration files alone.

Enterprise-Grade Architecture: The DDD hexagonal architecture with strict dependency rules is unique among Java AI agent frameworks. This architectural rigor makes Zhuling suitable for enterprise deployments where maintainability, testability, and separation of concerns are non-negotiable.

Comprehensive MCP Support: Supporting all three MCP modes (Local in-process Java tools, SSE remote MCP servers, and Stdio command-line MCP servers) gives Zhuling maximum flexibility for tool integration. Local MCP tools can be plain Java beans, while SSE and Stdio modes enable integration with external services and command-line tools.

Built-in Observable Chat UI: Zhuling ships with an observable chat interface that provides immediate visual feedback during development. Developers can interact with their agents, inspect tool calls, and debug behavior without deploying a separate frontend application.

What Are Zhuling’s Current Limitations?

Project Maturity: Zhuling was created on July 28, 2026 — less than 48 hours old at the time of this review. It has zero GitHub stars, no community, no issue tracker history, and no proven track record in production. Early adopters should expect bugs, breaking changes, and incomplete documentation.

Dependency on Snapshot Versions: The framework depends on Spring AI 2.0.1-SNAPSHOT, which is a pre-release version. This means Zhuling’s behavior may change as Spring AI’s APIs evolve, and production deployments may face compatibility issues when the stable release ships.

Limited Multi-Agent Capabilities: While Zhuling’s roadmap includes multi-agent collaboration (Phase 7), this feature is still in development. Competitors like Spring AI Alibaba (graph-based multi-agent) and Koog (mature multi-agent support) already offer production-ready multi-agent orchestration.

No Community or Ecosystem: With no contributors beyond the original developer, Zhuling lacks the community-driven plugins, extensions, and troubleshooting resources that frameworks like LangChain4j and Spring AI Alibaba offer. Documentation is limited to the README.

JDK 21 Requirement: Requiring JDK 21+ may be a barrier for organizations still on JDK 17 or 11. While JDK 21 adoption is growing, many enterprise Java shops have not yet migrated.

What Is Zhuling’s Development Roadmap?

Zhuling’s development is organized into 10 phases, with Phases 1 through 6.6 already complete:

Phase Focus Status
1 Basic project scaffolding and SpringBoot integration ✅ Complete
2 LLM service abstraction and provider support ✅ Complete
3 Tool calling framework and MCP integration ✅ Complete
4 Agent configuration system (YAML-based) ✅ Complete
5 Memory and conversation management ✅ Complete
6 Observable chat UI and debugging tools ✅ Complete
6.6 Multi-agent runtime foundation ✅ Complete
7 ReAct agent pattern implementation 🔄 In Progress
8 Multi-agent collaboration and orchestration 🔄 In Progress
9 Multimodal support (vision, audio) 🔄 In Progress
10 Testing framework, benchmarks, and production hardening 🔄 In Progress

The completed phases already deliver a functional single-agent framework with tool calling, MCP support, and observable UI. The in-progress phases (7-10) will add ReAct reasoning, multi-agent collaboration, multimodal capabilities, and production-grade testing — features that would make Zhuling competitive with established frameworks.

How Can Java Developers Get Started with Zhuling?

Getting started with Zhuling requires JDK 21+ and Maven 3.8+. The basic workflow is:

  1. Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/Vinist123/zhuling.git
  2. Configure an agent: Create a YAML file defining the agent’s model, tools, and skills
  3. Run the application: Use Maven to build and start the Spring Boot application
  4. Interact via chat UI: Access the built-in observable chat interface to test the agent
  5. Add custom tools: Implement Java classes for local MCP tools or connect to remote MCP servers via SSE/Stdio

The framework supports all OpenAI-compatible LLM services, including OpenAI, Tongyi Qianwen, Zhipu AI, Moonshot, and proxy services. This means developers are not locked into a single provider and can switch models by changing a YAML configuration value.

FAQ

Q1: Is Zhuling production-ready for enterprise use? A1: Not yet. Zhuling is less than 2 days old as of this review. While its architecture is enterprise-grade (DDD hexagonal, Spring Boot-native), the framework lacks production testing, community validation, and stability guarantees. It is best suited for experimentation and prototyping in its current state.

Q2: How does Zhuling compare to Spring AI Alibaba? A2: Spring AI Alibaba has 10,463+ GitHub stars, deep Alibaba Cloud integration, and mature multi-agent graph orchestration. Zhuling’s advantages are zero-code YAML configuration, DDD hexagonal architecture, and comprehensive MCP support. Spring AI Alibaba is production-ready; Zhuling is experimental.

Q3: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and why does it matter? A3: MCP is a protocol for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources. Zhuling supports three MCP modes: Local (in-process Java tools), SSE (remote servers via Server-Sent Events), and Stdio (command-line processes). This flexibility allows agents to access databases, APIs, file systems, and custom business logic through a standardized interface.

Q4: Can I use Zhuling without writing any Java code? A4: For basic agent configuration, yes — agents can be defined entirely through YAML files. However, custom tool implementations require Java classes, and advanced use cases (custom MCP servers, complex orchestration logic) will require Java development. The “zero-code” claim applies to agent definition, not to all aspects of the framework.

Q5: What LLM providers does Zhuling support? A5: Zhuling supports all OpenAI-compatible LLM services, including OpenAI (GPT-4o, GPT-4, etc.), Alibaba’s Tongyi Qianwen, Zhipu AI, Moonshot, and any proxy service that implements the OpenAI API specification. Provider configuration is done through YAML, making it easy to switch between models without code changes.

item.title: AI Agent Framework Comparison 2026: Mastra vs Agno vs LangGraph vs CrewAI
item.description: Compare the top 4 AI agent frameworks of 2026 — Mastra, Agno, LangGraph, and CrewAI — across language support, orchestration, production readiness, and community size.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction — The AI Agent Framework Landscape in 2026

The AI agent framework landscape in 2026 has matured dramatically from the experimental AutoGPT era of 2023. Four frameworks now dominate the conversation: Mastra (26.4k GitHub stars), Agno (41.3k stars), LangGraph (37.7k stars), and CrewAI (55.9k stars). Each takes a fundamentally different approach to building, orchestrating, and deploying AI agents. This AI agent framework comparison 2026 guide breaks down their architectures, strengths, weaknesses, and ideal use cases so you can choose the right tool for your next project.

Why Agent Frameworks Matter — From AutoGPT to Production-Grade Systems

The shift from experimental single-agent prototypes to production-grade multi-agent systems has been the defining trend of 2024–2026. Early frameworks like AutoGPT proved that LLM-driven agents could autonomously pursue goals, but they lacked the reliability, state management, and observability that enterprises demand.

Today’s agent frameworks solve four critical problems:

  1. Orchestration — Coordinating multiple agents that communicate, delegate, and hand off tasks
  2. State management — Persisting conversation history, tool outputs, and agent memory across sessions
  3. Tool integration — Connecting agents to APIs, databases, and external services with reliable function calling
  4. Observability — Tracing agent decisions, LLM calls, and tool executions for debugging and compliance

According to the CrewAI 2026 State of Agentic AI Survey, 65% of enterprises already use AI agents, and 81% are scaling them across teams. The question is no longer whether to adopt agent frameworks — it’s which one to standardize on.

Framework Deep Dives

Mastra — The TypeScript-Native Contender (26.4k ★)

Mastra launched in August 2024 and has rapidly grown to 26.4k GitHub stars with 2.5k forks. It is the only major framework built from the ground up for TypeScript, making it the default choice for JavaScript/TypeScript development teams.

Key features:

  • Native TypeScript support with full type safety across agent definitions, tools, and workflows
  • Built-in observability via Mastra Studio — a visual debugger for agent traces and LLM calls
  • Workflow engine supporting sequential, parallel, and conditional execution paths
  • Memory management with support for working memory, long-term storage, and semantic recall
  • First-class deployment integrations with Vercel, Cloudflare Workers, and Node.js servers

Mastra’s strength is its developer experience for TypeScript teams. If your stack is built on Next.js, Node.js, or any JS/TS ecosystem, Mastra integrates without introducing a new language. Its built-in observability tooling means you don’t need to bolt on a separate monitoring solution.

Best for: TypeScript/JavaScript teams, full-stack developers, projects that need built-in observability from day one.

Limitations: Smaller community than CrewAI or LangGraph; Python teams will need to maintain a separate stack; fewer production case studies compared to more mature frameworks.

Agno — SDK + Runtime Separation (41.3k ★)

Agno (formerly Phidata) has taken a unique architectural stance: it separates the agent framework (Agno SDK) from the agent runtime (AgentOS). This decoupling is the most forward-looking design in the current landscape.

Key features:

  • Agno SDK — A Python framework for defining agents, tools, workflows, and knowledge bases
  • AgentOS — A framework-agnostic runtime/control plane for deploying, monitoring, and managing agents in production
  • Multi-agent orchestration with role-based delegation and parallel execution
  • Built-in knowledge base integration with vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate)
  • Tool-calling reliability improvements over raw LLM function calling

Agno’s core insight, articulated in their blog post “The Framework Wars Are Over (And Nobody Won),” is that switching costs are high because most frameworks bundle orchestration code with deployment infrastructure. By decoupling the two, Agno lets teams switch orchestration patterns — or even frameworks — without re-platforming their production infrastructure.

Best for: Teams that value architectural flexibility, Python-heavy organizations, projects that need framework-agnostic production infrastructure.

Limitations: AgentOS is newer and has fewer battle-tested deployments; the two-component architecture adds conceptual overhead; smaller ecosystem of community-built tools compared to LangGraph or CrewAI.

LangGraph — Low-Level Orchestration Powerhouse (37.7k ★)

LangGraph, built by the LangChain team, is the most powerful and flexible agent orchestration framework available. With 37.7k GitHub stars and 6.3k forks, it has the deepest integration with the LangChain ecosystem.

Key features:

  • Graph-based state machine architecture — agents are nodes, transitions are edges
  • Full control over agent state, routing, and execution flow
  • Built-in persistence with checkpointing, thread-level state, and human-in-the-loop support
  • LangSmith integration for production-grade observability and tracing
  • Used in production by Klarna, Uber, and J.P. Morgan

LangGraph’s graph-based approach gives developers complete control over agent behavior. You define nodes (agent actions, tool calls, decision points) and edges (transitions between nodes), creating a directed graph that the runtime executes. This makes it ideal for complex workflows where agents must follow strict business logic, maintain state across multiple turns, or support human approval gates.

Best for: Complex multi-agent orchestration, production systems requiring fine-grained control, teams already invested in the LangChain ecosystem.

Limitations: Steepest learning curve of all four frameworks; graph-based programming model is unfamiliar to many developers; heavier boilerplate for simple use cases; LangChain dependency chain can be complex to manage.

CrewAI — The Community Favorite for Multi-Agent (55.9k ★)

CrewAI is the most popular AI agent framework by GitHub stars (55.9k) and forks (7.9k). Its role-based abstraction — where you define agents with roles, goals, and backstories — makes multi-agent systems intuitive and accessible.

Key features:

  • Role-based agent design — define agents as “researcher,” “writer,” “critic” with specific goals
  • Built-in task delegation and hierarchical process management
  • Sequential and hierarchical workflow patterns
  • Integration with over 1,000+ tools via the CrewAI tool ecosystem
  • YAML-based configuration for agent and task definitions

CrewAI’s strength is its simplicity. A developer can define a multi-agent research team in under 50 lines of code. The role-playing abstraction maps naturally to business workflows — a marketing team with a strategist, copywriter, and editor translates directly into CrewAI agents.

Best for: Rapid prototyping, role-based multi-agent scenarios, teams new to agent development, projects that need to ship quickly.

Limitations: Opinionated architecture limits customization for complex workflows; less suitable for production systems requiring fine-grained state control; performance overhead from the abstraction layer; fewer built-in observability features compared to Mastra or LangGraph.

Head-to-Head Comparison Matrix

Feature Mastra Agno LangGraph CrewAI
Language TypeScript Python Python Python
GitHub Stars 26.4k 41.3k 37.7k 55.9k
Forks 2.5k 5.7k 6.3k 7.9k
Release Year 2024 2023 (rebranded 2025) 2024 2023
Orchestration Model Workflow engine SDK + Runtime Graph-based state machine Role-based agents
Built-in Observability Yes (Mastra Studio) Yes (AgentOS) Yes (LangSmith) Limited (third-party)
Memory/State Working + long-term Knowledge base + memory Checkpointing + threads Task-based context
Production Deployments Growing Early Klarna, Uber, J.P. Morgan Many startups
Learning Curve Low-Medium Medium High Low
Best For TypeScript teams Flexible architecture Complex orchestration Rapid prototyping

Language Support (TypeScript vs Python)

The language divide is the single most important decision factor. Mastra is the only TypeScript-native framework, while Agno, LangGraph, and CrewAI are all Python-first.

For TypeScript/JavaScript teams, Mastra eliminates the need to maintain a separate Python codebase for agent development. It integrates naturally with Next.js, Node.js, Vercel, and Cloudflare Workers — the modern full-stack JavaScript stack.

Python teams have three strong options. Agno offers the most architectural flexibility with its SDK + runtime separation. LangGraph provides the deepest control for complex workflows. CrewAI delivers the fastest path from idea to working prototype.

The choice often comes down to your team’s existing expertise. A Node.js backend team will find Mastra’s TypeScript-native approach dramatically more productive than learning Python and the LangChain ecosystem.

Learning Curve & Developer Experience

CrewAI wins on ease of use. Its role-based abstraction is intuitive — anyone who has worked in a team can understand “researcher agent,” “writer agent,” “critic agent.” The YAML configuration format makes agent definitions readable and maintainable.

Mastra offers a close second, especially for TypeScript developers. Type safety catches errors at compile time, and the built-in Studio provides visual debugging that reduces iteration time.

Agno sits in the middle. The SDK is straightforward, but the two-component architecture (SDK + AgentOS) requires understanding a broader mental model.

LangGraph has the steepest learning curve. The graph-based state machine model is powerful but requires a paradigm shift for most developers. You’re not writing linear code — you’re defining nodes, edges, routing functions, and state schemas. The payoff is complete control, but the upfront investment is significant.

Production Readiness & Deployment

LangGraph leads in production readiness, with documented deployments at Klarna, Uber, and J.P. Morgan. Its checkpointing, human-in-the-loop support, and LangSmith observability make it suitable for regulated industries.

Mastra’s built-in deployment integrations with Vercel and Cloudflare Workers make it the easiest to deploy for web applications. The Mastra Studio provides production-grade observability without additional infrastructure.

Agno’s AgentOS is designed specifically for production deployment, with a control plane for monitoring, scaling, and managing agents. However, it’s newer and has fewer documented large-scale deployments.

CrewAI is widely used in production by startups and mid-market companies, but its opinionated architecture can be a limitation for complex enterprise requirements. The lack of built-in observability means teams need to add their own monitoring.

Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns

The four frameworks take fundamentally different approaches to multi-agent orchestration:

  • LangGraph uses a graph-based state machine where agents are nodes and transitions are edges. This gives maximum control but requires explicit definition of every state and transition.

  • CrewAI uses role-based hierarchical orchestration. Agents have roles, goals, and backstories, and tasks are assigned through sequential or hierarchical processes.

  • Agno supports role-based delegation with parallel execution, plus the ability to switch orchestration patterns through its decoupled architecture.

  • Mastra uses a workflow engine with sequential, parallel, and conditional execution paths, all defined in TypeScript with full type safety.

For simple sequential workflows, all four frameworks work well. For complex branching logic with conditional routing, LangGraph’s graph model excels. For rapid multi-agent prototyping, CrewAI’s role-based approach is unmatched.

Memory, State & Persistence

Memory management is a critical differentiator for production agent systems:

  • LangGraph offers the most sophisticated state management with checkpointing, thread-level persistence, and the ability to pause/resume agent execution. This is essential for long-running agent workflows.

  • Agno provides knowledge base integration with vector databases and built-in memory management, making it strong for RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) use cases.

  • Mastra supports working memory (short-term context) and long-term storage with semantic recall, suitable for most conversational agent use cases.

  • CrewAI uses task-based context passing — agents share information through task outputs. This works well for sequential workflows but is less suitable for agents that need persistent memory across sessions.

Observability & Monitoring

Observability is where the frameworks diverge most:

  • Mastra Studio provides visual debugging of agent traces, LLM calls, and tool executions out of the box. No additional setup required.

  • LangGraph integrates with LangSmith for comprehensive tracing, monitoring, and evaluation. LangSmith is a separate product but deeply integrated.

  • Agno includes observability through AgentOS, with monitoring dashboards and execution traces.

  • CrewAI has limited built-in observability. Teams typically add Langfuse, LangSmith, or custom logging.

For teams that prioritize debugging and monitoring, Mastra’s built-in Studio and LangGraph’s LangSmith integration provide the most polished experiences.

Community & Ecosystem Size

CrewAI leads with 55.9k GitHub stars and the largest community. This translates to more tutorials, community-built tools, and faster answers to questions.

LangGraph benefits from the broader LangChain ecosystem, which includes LangSmith, LangServe, and extensive documentation. The LangChain community is one of the largest in the AI development space.

Agno (41.3k stars) has a growing community, particularly among developers interested in the decoupled architecture approach.

Mastra (26.4k stars) has the smallest community but is growing rapidly. Its TypeScript focus means it attracts a different developer demographic than the Python-dominated alternatives.

The Framework Wars Are Over — Orchestration vs. Runtime Decoupling

Agno’s provocative thesis — that the framework wars are over and nobody won — captures a crucial insight. The real architectural distinction isn’t between frameworks but between orchestration and runtime.

Most frameworks bundle both layers together. When you build with CrewAI, you’re locked into CrewAI’s deployment model. When you build with LangGraph, you’re locked into the LangChain ecosystem. This bundling creates high switching costs — migrating from one framework to another means rewriting both your agent logic and your deployment infrastructure.

Agno’s AgentOS is the first serious attempt to decouple these layers. AgentOS provides a framework-agnostic runtime that can execute agents built with any orchestration framework. If you build your agent logic with Agno SDK but deploy on AgentOS, you can theoretically switch to a different orchestration pattern without touching your production infrastructure.

This decoupling pattern mirrors the evolution of web development, where frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) are separate from deployment platforms (Vercel, Netlify, AWS). The same separation is now emerging in the agent framework space.

Enterprise Adoption Trends — What the 2026 Data Says

The CrewAI 2026 State of Agentic AI Survey, conducted among 500 senior enterprise executives, reveals a market at an inflection point:

  • 100% of surveyed enterprises plan to expand agentic AI adoption in 2026
  • 65% are already using AI agents in production
  • 81% are scaling agent deployments across multiple teams
  • 75% report high or very high impact on time savings
  • 69% cite significant operational cost reductions
  • 34% rank security and governance as the top evaluation factor for agentic platforms
  • 57% prefer building on existing open-source tools rather than building from scratch

The security and governance finding is particularly significant. In 2024 and 2025, the primary evaluation criteria were raw capability and ease of use. In 2026, enterprises are prioritizing security, compliance, and governance — a sign that agentic AI has moved from experimental to mission-critical.

How to Choose the Right Framework for Your Use Case

Choose Mastra if: Your team is TypeScript/JavaScript-native, you want built-in observability without additional tooling, or you’re deploying on Vercel/Cloudflare Workers.

Choose Agno if: You value architectural flexibility, want to decouple orchestration from runtime, or need strong knowledge base/RAG integration.

Choose LangGraph if: You’re building complex multi-agent systems with strict state management requirements, need human-in-the-loop workflows, or are already invested in the LangChain ecosystem.

Choose CrewAI if: You need to prototype and ship multi-agent systems quickly, your use case maps naturally to role-based agents, or you want the largest community and ecosystem.

For most teams, the decision comes down to language preference (TypeScript vs. Python) and complexity requirements. Simple to moderately complex agent systems can be built with any framework. For production systems with complex state management, LangGraph or Mastra are the strongest choices. For rapid experimentation and prototyping, CrewAI is unmatched.

Conclusion — The Future of AI Agent Frameworks

The AI agent framework landscape in 2026 is defined by four strong contenders, each with a distinct architectural philosophy. Mastra brings TypeScript-native development with built-in observability. Agno pioneers the orchestration-runtime decoupling. LangGraph offers unmatched control for complex production systems. CrewAI makes multi-agent development accessible to everyone.

The most important trend is the maturation of the ecosystem. Enterprise adoption has reached a tipping point — 100% of enterprises plan to expand agentic AI in 2026. Security and governance have overtaken raw capability as the primary evaluation criteria. And the architectural debate is shifting from “which framework” to “how to decouple orchestration from runtime.”

As the market matures, expect to see more convergence on the decoupled architecture that Agno is pioneering, with frameworks specializing in orchestration while runtimes specialize in production deployment. The framework wars may indeed be over — but the real battle for production-grade agent infrastructure is just beginning.

FAQ

Q1: What is the best AI agent framework in 2026? A: There is no single “best” framework — the right choice depends on your team’s language preference, complexity requirements, and deployment needs. Mastra is best for TypeScript teams, LangGraph for complex orchestration, CrewAI for rapid prototyping, and Agno for architectural flexibility.

Q2: Is CrewAI better than LangGraph? A: CrewAI is better for rapid prototyping and role-based multi-agent scenarios, while LangGraph is better for complex production systems requiring fine-grained state control. CrewAI has more GitHub stars (55.9k vs 37.7k), but LangGraph has more production deployments at enterprise scale.

Q3: Can I use Mastra with Python? A: No — Mastra is TypeScript-native and does not support Python. If your team uses Python, consider Agno, LangGraph, or CrewAI instead.

Q4: What is the difference between agent orchestration and agent runtime? A: Orchestration refers to how agents are defined, coordinated, and how they communicate. Runtime refers to the production infrastructure for deploying, monitoring, and scaling agents. Most frameworks bundle both, but Agno’s AgentOS decouples them, allowing teams to switch orchestration patterns without changing deployment infrastructure.

Q5: How do I choose between Agno and CrewAI? A: Choose Agno if you value architectural flexibility, want to decouple orchestration from runtime, or need strong knowledge base integration. Choose CrewAI if you need to prototype quickly, prefer role-based agent abstractions, or want the largest community and ecosystem.

item.title: AWS Strands Agents SDK: Build Production AI Agents in 2026
item.description: Complete guide to AWS Strands Agents SDK — install, build, deploy, and monitor production AI agents with minimal code in 2026.

AWS Strands Agents is an open-source Python and TypeScript SDK that lets you build production-ready AI agents in under 10 lines of code. Released by AWS in May 2025 and reaching 14 million+ downloads, it uses a model-driven loop where you describe a goal, attach tools, and the agent decides at runtime what to call and in what order.

What Is AWS Strands Agents SDK?

AWS Strands Agents SDK is an open-source AI agent framework developed by Amazon Web Services that uses a model-driven paradigm — you describe what you want the agent to achieve, attach a set of tools, and the underlying LLM decides which tools to call, in which order, and when to stop. Unlike graph-based frameworks that require you to wire explicit nodes and edges, Strands agents reason dynamically at runtime, adapting their execution plan based on intermediate results. Since its preview launch in May 2025, Strands has accumulated 14 million+ downloads and powers internal AWS services including Amazon Q Developer, AWS Glue, and the VPC Reachability Analyzer. The SDK supports 9+ model providers — Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, LiteLLM, Llama, Ollama, and Writer — through a unified API, so you can prototype locally with Ollama and deploy to Bedrock without touching your agent logic. Version 1.0 added Graph, Swarm, and Workflow multi-agent patterns and the A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol for cross-framework interoperability. The result is the lowest barrier-to-entry of any major agent framework available in 2026.

Why Strands Agents? Key Advantages Over Competitors

Strands Agents stands out from competing frameworks through three core design decisions: minimal API surface, native MCP support, and built-in observability. Where LangGraph requires you to define state schemas, build graph topologies, and wire conditional edges before writing any business logic, a functional Strands agent is four lines: import the SDK, declare tools with a decorator, instantiate an Agent, and call it with a string. Verisk Analytics deployed a RAG-backed Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock and reduced mean-time-to-resolution (MTTR) by 60% without any manual coding pipeline. That outcome is possible because Strands handles the entire agentic loop — tool selection, execution, result injection, and follow-up reasoning — automatically. The framework is also model-agnostic by design: switching from Claude Sonnet on Bedrock to GPT-4o on OpenAI is a one-line config change, not a framework migration. Finally, OpenTelemetry instrumentation is built in — every tool call, reasoning step, and model invocation emits traces and metrics without additional setup, routing natively to AWS X-Ray and CloudWatch. For teams already running workloads on AWS, this is a compelling stack: write minimal Python, deploy to Bedrock AgentCore, and get full observability for free.

When Strands Beats the Alternatives

Strands is the right choice when you want fast iteration, MCP tool reuse, or an AWS-native deployment path. If your workflow is deterministic and requires strict execution ordering with human-in-the-loop checkpoints, LangGraph’s state-machine model is stronger. If you’re organizing a large team of specialized agents with a crew/role mental model, CrewAI’s abstractions are more intuitive for product managers. For everything else — especially when MCP tool servers already exist for your data sources — Strands wins on productivity.

Installation and Quick Start (Python & TypeScript)

Installing AWS Strands Agents takes under a minute and requires no AWS account for local development with Ollama. For Python, run pip install strands-agents and optionally pip install strands-agents-tools for the 30+ built-in tools. For TypeScript, run npm install @strands/agents. A minimal working agent in Python requires four lines of code: import Agent and tool, decorate a function with @tool, create agent = Agent(tools=[your_tool]), and call agent("your prompt"). The agent calls your tool as many times as needed, reasons about the results, and returns a final answer — no graph, no state schema, no chain. For production use with Amazon Bedrock, set AWS_DEFAULT_REGION and install strands-agents[bedrock]; for Anthropic, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and pass model=AnthropicModel("claude-sonnet-4-6") to the Agent constructor. The model-swap is the only change required; all tool definitions, agent logic, and multi-agent patterns remain identical across providers.

Your First Agent in Python

from strands import Agent, tool

@tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Return current weather for a city."""
    return f"{city}: 22°C, partly cloudy"

agent = Agent(tools=[get_weather])
response = agent("What's the weather in Berlin?")
print(response)

That is a complete, runnable agent. Add a model= parameter to switch providers; add more @tool functions to expand capabilities. The agent loop handles everything else.

TypeScript Quick Start

import { Agent, tool } from "@strands/agents";
import { z } from "zod";

const getWeather = tool({
  name: "get_weather",
  description: "Return current weather for a city",
  parameters: z.object({ city: z.string() }),
  execute: async ({ city }) => `${city}: 22°C, partly cloudy`,
});

const agent = new Agent({ tools: [getWeather] });
await agent.run("What's the weather in Berlin?");

Core Concepts: Tools, Model Providers, and the Agent Loop

The Strands agent loop is the runtime engine that drives all agent behavior: it feeds the user prompt and tool definitions to the model, receives tool-call responses, executes the designated tools, injects results back into the conversation context, and repeats until the model emits a final text response with no pending tool calls. This loop is fully managed — you never write it manually. Tools are the primary extension point: any Python function decorated with @tool automatically becomes callable by the model. The SDK introspects the function’s type annotations and docstring to auto-generate the JSON Schema that Strands passes to the model, so documentation doubles as the tool spec. Model providers are swappable at Agent instantiation time: BedrockModel, AnthropicModel, OpenAIModel, OllamaModel, and others all implement the same interface. The agent loop itself does not care which model is running; only the model= parameter changes. For advanced control, you can set max_parallel_tool_calls, configure system_prompt, and attach callbacks for streaming output or custom logging — all without modifying the loop itself. This clean separation of concerns is what makes Strands agents easy to test and maintain at production scale.

Understanding Tool Execution

When the model decides to call a tool, Strands validates the arguments against the tool’s schema, executes the function (sync or async), and serializes the return value back into the conversation. If the model requests multiple tools simultaneously, Strands executes them in parallel by default, then batches the results into a single context injection. This parallelism is transparent — your tool functions do not need to know about concurrency.

Built-in Tool Ecosystem and MCP Integration

Strands ships with 30+ production-ready tools in the strands-agents-tools package covering file operations, HTTP requests, shell execution, Python REPL, database queries, image analysis, and AWS service calls (S3, DynamoDB, Lambda invoke). Beyond built-ins, Strands has first-class Model Context Protocol (MCP) support — you can connect any MCP server to your agent with three lines of code and instantly access thousands of community-built tool servers covering GitHub, Slack, Postgres, Notion, and hundreds of other services. This MCP-first design means you rarely need to write custom tools for standard integrations. The pattern is: create an MCPClient pointing at your MCP server URL, call .list_tools() to get the tool list, and pass the list to Agent(tools=mcp_tools). The agent treats MCP tools identically to native @tool functions — same loop, same observability, same parallelism. Practically, this means a team can build an agent that queries a Postgres database, creates GitHub issues, and sends Slack notifications using only MCP servers, with zero custom integration code and full OTEL tracing on every call.

from strands import Agent
from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient

with MCPClient("http://localhost:8080") as mcp:
    tools = mcp.list_tools()
    agent = Agent(tools=tools)
    agent("Query the last 10 orders from the database")

Connecting a new data source becomes a matter of running an MCP server — no bespoke integration code required.

Multi-Agent Patterns: Graph, Swarm, and Workflow

Strands Agents 1.0 introduced three structured multi-agent patterns that cover the most common production topologies: Graph, Swarm, and Workflow. Graph mode lets you define explicit agent nodes and directed edges, giving you deterministic control over which agent hands off to which — useful when you need auditability or strict sequencing for compliance. Swarm mode spins up a pool of identical worker agents that pull tasks from a shared queue; each worker operates independently and reports back to a coordinator, making Swarm ideal for embarrassingly parallel workloads like bulk document processing or parallel API calls across accounts. Workflow mode is the simplest: a linear pipeline where each agent’s output becomes the next agent’s input, perfect for ETL-style tasks (extract → transform → load) or document processing pipelines (ingest → summarize → classify → store). All three patterns use the same underlying Agent primitive and the same tool and model interfaces — the pattern controls topology, not implementation. The A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol allows agents built with different frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, custom REST services) to be treated as tools by a Strands orchestrator, so you are not locked in even at the multi-agent layer. Each pattern ships with built-in session management, so state is durable across invocations.

Using the Handoff Primitive

The handoff primitive passes control to another agent or a human reviewer without terminating the session. This is the key building block for human-in-the-loop workflows: an agent completes as much work as possible autonomously, then hands off to a human when it encounters ambiguity, and resumes when the human responds. Handoffs are serializable — the session state is stored in the Session Manager (backed by DynamoDB or any key-value store) so the resuming agent picks up exactly where the previous one stopped.

Deploying to Production: Lambda, Fargate, and Bedrock AgentCore

Strands agents can be deployed to AWS Lambda for short-lived event-driven tasks, AWS Fargate for long-running streaming agents, or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for a fully managed production path with built-in identity, memory, observability, and tool integration. Lambda deployments suit agents with sub-15-minute execution windows and sporadic invocation patterns — the pay-per-request model is cost-efficient at low to medium scale. Fargate is the right target when agents need to stream responses in real time or when execution windows exceed Lambda’s limit; a recommended architecture uses API Gateway fronting a Fargate container running the agent loop, with Lambda functions backing individual tools. Bedrock AgentCore is AWS’s managed runtime for Strands agents: it eliminates infrastructure provisioning, handles auto-scaling, provides persistent session storage, and integrates Strands observability with CloudWatch and X-Ray automatically. For enterprise teams, AgentCore is the fastest path from prototype to production because it removes the need to manage container registries, IAM roles for tool execution, or session storage backends. A typical Fargate-hosted streaming agent can be wired up in under 30 lines of FastAPI code and deployed as a Docker container with a standard ECS task definition.

# Fargate: expose agent as streaming HTTP endpoint
from fastapi import FastAPI
from strands import Agent
from strands.models import BedrockModel

app = FastAPI()
agent = Agent(model=BedrockModel("us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6-v1"))

@app.post("/run")
async def run_agent(prompt: str):
    async for chunk in agent.stream(prompt):
        yield chunk

For Lambda, package the agent with a handler that instantiates Agent per invocation and returns the agent(event["prompt"]) response as JSON.

Bedrock AgentCore Deployment

from strands.deploy import BedrockAgentCore

core = BedrockAgentCore(
    agent=agent,
    region="us-east-1",
    memory_backend="dynamodb",
)
core.deploy()  # provisions all infrastructure

AgentCore handles IAM, VPC, scaling policies, and CloudWatch dashboards automatically.

Observability and Monitoring with OpenTelemetry

Strands Agents ships with built-in OpenTelemetry instrumentation that requires zero configuration to activate — every agent invocation automatically emits spans for model calls, tool executions, and reasoning steps. This matters because AI agent debugging without traces is guesswork: you need to see which tools were called, in what order, with what arguments, and how long each step took. Strands traces integrate natively with AWS X-Ray (via the OTEL OTLP exporter pointing at the X-Ray collector), CloudWatch (via the CloudWatch OTEL Distro), and any third-party backend that accepts OTLP — Grafana, Jaeger, or Datadog. Fan-out routing is supported, so you can send traces to X-Ray for the AWS console while simultaneously forwarding to Grafana for team dashboards. Custom attributes added via standard OTEL APIs propagate through multi-agent chains, so a root trace from an orchestrator spans all downstream worker agent calls. Metrics include token counts per call, tool latency by name, and agent loop iteration counts — all available in CloudWatch without any custom metric publishing code. In practice, a Strands agent with three tools on Bedrock produces full end-to-end traces in X-Ray within the first invocation, with no instrumentation code written by the developer.

from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.exporter.otlp.proto.grpc.trace_exporter import OTLPSpanExporter

provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(OTLPSpanExporter()))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)

# Strands automatically picks up the configured OTEL provider
agent = Agent(tools=[...])

No Strands-specific configuration needed — standard OTEL SDK setup is sufficient.

Strands Agents vs LangGraph vs CrewAI: Which Should You Use?

Strands Agents, LangGraph, and CrewAI each occupy a distinct position in the 2026 AI agent landscape, and the right choice depends on your workflow type, team composition, and deployment target. Strands is optimized for minimal code, fast iteration, and AWS-native deployment: it’s the strongest choice for teams building on Bedrock, leveraging MCP tools, or needing to prototype and ship quickly. LangGraph is a production-grade state-machine framework — more verbose, but the most battle-tested option for complex deterministic workflows where execution order must be auditable and human-in-the-loop checkpoints are required at defined graph nodes. CrewAI uses a crew/role abstraction that maps well to organizational structures; product managers and non-engineers find it easier to reason about than graphs or loops. The critical differentiator for 2026: Strands is the only framework with a direct managed deployment target (Bedrock AgentCore) that eliminates infrastructure entirely, and it is the only one with MCP-first design that connects to community tool servers without custom code. Strands reached 1 million downloads and 3,000+ GitHub stars within just four months of its preview launch, a pace that signals strong developer adoption and active community investment.

Feature Strands Agents LangGraph CrewAI
Learning curve Low (4 lines to start) High (graph topology) Medium (crew/role model)
Model agnostic Yes (9+ providers) Yes Yes
MCP support Native, first-class Via LangChain tools Via custom adapters
Managed deployment Bedrock AgentCore LangSmith Cloud CrewAI Cloud
Multi-agent patterns Graph, Swarm, Workflow Graph, subgraphs Crew, pipeline
Built-in observability OTEL, X-Ray, CloudWatch LangSmith tracing Built-in logs
Best for AWS workloads, fast iteration Complex deterministic flows Role-based team simulations

When to Stick With LangGraph

LangGraph remains the strongest choice when your workflow has complex conditional branching that must be fully deterministic — financial compliance pipelines, multi-step approval workflows, or any scenario where the execution graph needs to be audited after the fact. Its visual debugger in LangSmith is more mature than Strands tooling as of mid-2026.

Real-World Use Cases and Enterprise Adoption

AWS Strands Agents has moved beyond early-adopter experimentation into enterprise production deployments. Amazon internal teams run it at scale: Amazon Q Developer uses Strands for IDE assistant workflows, AWS Glue uses it for automated ETL pipeline generation, and the VPC Reachability Analyzer uses Strands agents to diagnose complex network configurations. Outside AWS, Verisk Analytics — a Fortune 500 data analytics company serving the insurance industry — deployed a Strands-based RAG agent on Amazon Bedrock that reduced mean-time-to-resolution for data engineering incidents by 60%, entirely without manual coding pipelines. The pattern driving these results is consistent: Strands agents connect to existing data sources via MCP (replacing bespoke integrations), reason over retrieved context, and take actions through typed tools with full OTEL tracing on every step. Common enterprise patterns in production as of 2026 include DevOps agents that triage CloudWatch alarms and auto-remediate known failure modes, data engineering agents that generate and deploy Glue jobs from natural-language specs, and customer support agents that query CRM systems and escalate to humans when confidence is below threshold. The SDK’s 14 million+ total downloads indicate these patterns are being replicated broadly across organizations already running on AWS infrastructure.

Patterns Worth Reusing

The most reusable Strands pattern is the “read-reason-act” loop backed by a Session Manager: the agent reads current state (from DynamoDB, S3, or an MCP database tool), reasons about the delta between current and desired state, and calls action tools to close the gap. Session state is persisted after each loop iteration, so the agent can be interrupted and resumed across Lambda invocations without losing context.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Is AWS Strands Agents free and open source? Yes. Strands Agents SDK is Apache-2.0 licensed and available on GitHub at strands-agents/sdk-python and strands-agents/sdk-js. There is no cost to use the framework itself. You pay only for model inference (Bedrock, OpenAI, etc.) and any AWS infrastructure you deploy to (Lambda, Fargate, AgentCore).

Q: Does Strands Agents require Amazon Bedrock? No. Bedrock is one of 9+ supported model providers, but Strands works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama, and others out of the box. You can build and run agents entirely locally using Ollama without any AWS account or credentials.

Q: How does Strands Agents handle long-running tasks that exceed Lambda’s timeout? Use Fargate for the agent loop (no timeout) and Lambda for individual tool executions. The recommended production architecture is API Gateway → Fargate (agent loop) → Lambda (tools), which lets you scale tool execution independently of the main loop. Alternatively, use the Session Manager to checkpoint state and continue across multiple Lambda invocations.

Q: Can Strands Agents work with agents built on other frameworks like LangGraph or CrewAI? Yes, via the A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol introduced in Strands 1.0. Any agent exposing an A2A-compliant endpoint can be invoked as a tool by a Strands orchestrator. This enables hybrid architectures where a Strands orchestrator coordinates LangGraph sub-agents for complex deterministic sub-tasks.

Q: What’s the difference between Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock Agents (the managed console feature)? Amazon Bedrock Agents is a no-code/low-code managed service configured through the AWS console. Strands Agents SDK is a code-first framework that you deploy yourself — it gives you full control over agent logic, tool definitions, and deployment targets. Strands can deploy to Bedrock AgentCore (the managed runtime), but it is a distinct product from the console-based Bedrock Agents service.
